en-o17-corrections-2026-11-04.summary: Five facts corrected: a study animal, one FDA letter, a population, two glossary definitions and a label group.
en-o17-corrections-2026-11-04.detail: KPV: a mechanism step said the wound result was in rodents; the study was in rabbit corneas (Bonfiglio 2006). PT-141: the page said the FDA sent warning letters to several online sellers naming PT-141; we have verified one such letter, of 24 August 2026 (FDA warning-letters index). Retatrutide: the liver-fat study was in adults with obesity or overweight, not only obesity (Sanyal 2024). Glossary: “recreational athlete” is defined in the World Anti-Doping Code since 2021, not only from 2027 (WADA Code 2021); a “deletion sequence” misses building blocks, and a chain that stops too early is a separate impurity, a truncated sequence (EMA guideline on synthetic peptides, 2025). Semaglutide: for Wegovy, Poviztra and Sevmia in Canada and Wegovy and Poviztra in Australia, the teenage group now says obesity and a body weight above 60 kg, as the labels do.

en-advertising-review-2026-11-04.summary: Pages checked against the rule that a text must not praise a medicine; wording made balanced.
en-advertising-review-2026-11-04.detail: Courts in the country we publish from ruled in 2026 that a text can be advertising even when its writer sells nothing, if it praises a medicine. We checked the English pages against that rule. Where a page named an effect without its evidence level, uncertainty or risks, we added them; words such as “promising” in our own voice were replaced; approved medicines are described with the uses on their official labels, and use outside those uses is called off-label. The publisher line on the about pages now says this. No fact changed.

us-hhs-2026-peptide-policy.summary: US compounding of six peptides: brought up to date with the draft HHS policy of 30 October 2026.
us-hhs-2026-peptide-policy.detail: These pages said that compounding BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax and epitalon in the US stays prohibited until the FDA completes a rule. On 30 October 2026 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) published a draft policy: until a final rule decides on each, HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against pharmacies, federal facilities or licensed doctors that compound them under strict conditions. The pages now say so. The law has not changed: none of the six is on the 503A list, and on 3 November 2026 no rule had been proposed. The policy is not binding, approves nothing and changes nothing outside the US. Sources: the Federal Register notice FR Doc. 2026-22192 and the HHS policy.

tesamorelin-approval-answer.summary: Tesamorelin: “Is it an approved medicine?” now answers for each country, with the US approval and Canada’s.
tesamorelin-approval-answer.detail: Before, the answer started with the EU status and did not name the US, where tesamorelin has been an approved medicine since 10 November 2010. It also left out Canada. It now answers for each country: approved in the US; approved in Canada on 29 April 2014, but the company stopped selling it there on 30 September 2022; not approved in the UK or Australia. The dates come from the FDA and Health Canada and are shown, with their sources, in the status table on the page.
